extracted.intended_audience: petitioners, patent owners, and practitioners participating in PTAB inter partes review (IPR) proceedings; patent litigators and examiners
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis and determination of patent claim unpatentability in a United States PTAB inter partes review, applying claim construction, prior-art assessment, obviousness (Graham) factors, and evidentiary standards. Includes assessing expert testimony, intrinsic evidence, and secondary considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of proof — preponderance of the evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Petitioner has demonstrated, by a preponderance of the evidence, that claims 1–9 are unpatentable. (Final Written Decision pursuant to 35 U.S.C. § 318(a))
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An IPR petitioner must prove unpatentability by a preponderance of the evidence. The Board's final determination is based on whether the petitioner has met that burden for the challenged claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction standard
rubrics_metrics.description: We construe claims 'using the same claim construction standard that would be used to construe the claim in a civil action under 35 U.S.C. 282(b), including construing the claim in accordance with the ordinary and customary meaning of such claim as understood by one of ordinary skill in the art and the prosecution history pertaining to the patent.' (37 C.F.R. § 42.100(b); Phillips v. AWH Corp.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only terms 'in controversy' need express construction and only to the extent necessary to resolve the controversy (citing Nidec and Vivid). Use intrinsic evidence (claims, specification, prosecution history) to construe terms; do not adopt limiting constructions absent highly persuasive evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Level of ordinary skill in the art
rubrics_metrics.description: Define the person of ordinary skill in the art (POSITA) for the technology at issue (here, e.g., 'a bachelor’s degree in electrical engineering, computer engineering, computer science, or a similar field, along with one to two years of experience developing or programming video games or video game systems...').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board adopts a POSITA definition consistent with the patent and applied prior art. Less work experience may be compensated by a higher level of education or vice versa; small differences in proposed POSITA do not necessarily affect obviousness outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Printed publication status for IPR prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: A published patent application is a 'printed publication' for purposes of 35 U.S.C. § 311(b) and, by virtue of § 102(e)(1), can be deemed prior art as of its filing date (citing Lynk Labs v. Samsung).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing whether a reference is proper prior art for IPR, treat published patent applications as printed publications and account for their filing date where § 102(e)(1) applies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness legal framework — Graham factors
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is unpatentable under 35 U.S.C. § 103 if differences between the claimed subject matter and the prior art are such that the subject matter as a whole would have been obvious to a POSITA. Determine (1) scope and content of the prior art; (2) differences between claimed subject matter and prior art; (3) level of skill in the art; and (4) objective evidence of nonobviousness (secondary considerations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resolve obviousness on the basis of underlying factual determinations and apply legal reasoning (Graham v. John Deere). Address motivation to combine and reasonable expectation of success when combining references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and content of the prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate the teachings, disclosures, and specific embodiments of the asserted prior-art references (e.g., what Hays, van Datta, Levkovitz disclose regarding advertisement delivery, client requests, ad insertion, tagging of assets, bots/electronic agents, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze prior-art references in detail (figures, passages, examples) to determine whether they anticipate or render obvious specific claim limitations; cite specific paragraphs/figures as the record supports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differences between claims and prior art; reasons to modify or combine
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify any differences between the claimed limitations and the prior art and articulate why a skilled artisan would modify or combine references, with a rational underpinning, to arrive at the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A valid obviousness combination requires articulated reasons to combine references and, where relevant, a reasonable expectation of success; evidence of specific advantages or teachable motivations (e.g., user customization benefits) supports a motivation to combine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective indicia of nonobviousness (secondary considerations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider evidence such as long‑felt but unresolved need, commercial success, industry praise, unexpected results, and whether such evidence has a nexus to the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secondary considerations must be linked to the claimed features and weighed against the prior art; weak or non‑nexus evidence (e.g., where prior art already met the industry need) is entitled to little weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of specification and prosecution history in claim interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification and prosecution history are used to interpret claim terms, and examples in the specification may rebut overly narrow constructions (e.g., a preferred embodiment showing skins/ad updates that would be excluded by narrowing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not adopt a claim construction that excludes a preferred embodiment absent highly persuasive evidentiary support (Vitronics). Prosecution history may inform but does not automatically limit claim scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preamble and limitation analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether preamble language is limiting based on claim language, specification, and prosecution history; the Board need not decide whether a preamble is limiting if not necessary to resolve the controversy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether preamble provides essential structure/meaning to the claim or merely states intended use; litigation positions and record evidence guide whether to treat the preamble as a limitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credibility and weight of expert testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: Give weight to expert declarations consistent with the record and disregard testimony that is plainly inconsistent with the intrinsic or extrinsic record (citing Homeland Housewares).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate experts against documentary evidence and prior-art disclosures; inconsistencies with the record reduce or eliminate credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combining references — motivation and reasonable expectation
rubrics_metrics.description: When asserting obviousness based on multiple references, show why a POSITA would have been motivated to combine the teachings and have a reasonable expectation of success in doing so (e.g., van Datta’s teachings provide specific benefits of allowing a user to select ads that motivate combining with Hays).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board credits testimony and documentary support showing concrete advantages (e.g., customization, advertiser willingness to pay) that supply a rational underpinning for combination; arguments that references teach away or are 'agnostic' to a limitation must be supported by the references themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible grounds and scope for IPR challenges
rubrics_metrics.description: An IPR may be instituted only on grounds that could be raised under section 102 or 103 and only on the basis of prior art consisting of patents or printed publications (35 U.S.C. § 311(b)); institution is governed by 35 U.S.C. § 314.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure asserted grounds rely on patents or printed publications and meet statutory thresholds for institution; post-institution the Board proceeds to final written decision per § 318(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-decision procedural obligations and options
rubrics_metrics.description: Because this is a Final Written Decision, parties seeking judicial review must comply with notice and service requirements of 37 C.F.R. § 90.2. Patent Owner may pursue amendment via reissue or reexamination but must notify the Board of related matters in updated mandatory notices (37 C.F.R. § 42.8).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Litigation and post-IPR avenues (reissue/reexamination) have procedural requirements and ongoing disclosure obligations to the Board; see April 2019 Notice Regarding Options for Amendments.
